chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated from al-Nadr ibn Shu'ayb from Abd al-Ghaffar al-Jazi who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the person in ihram who is compelled by necessity to eat a dead animal, and he found one and also found game. He said: 'He eats the dead animal and leaves the game.' He mentioned that if you are in a state of halal (outside ihram) and you kill the game between al-Breed and al-Haram, then upon you is its compensation (fidyah). If you blind its eye, or break its horn, or wound it, you give charity.

key_terms.الْبَرِيدِ: A specific distance or region between Mecca and Medina, often cited in fiqh regarding ihram boundaries
key_terms.الْمَيْتَةِ: A dead animal (maytah) not slaughtered according to Islamic rites
key_terms.الْمُحْرِمِ: The person in the state of ihram (sacred consecration) for Hajj or Umrah

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a pilgrim in ihram who eats a dead animal out of necessity, and what compensation is due if they kill game?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) distinguishes between the permissibility of consuming a dead animal out of dire necessity while in ihram and the liability for killing game, emphasizing that the latter incurs a specific compensation (jaza') even if done outside the sacred precincts. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that the sanctity of the game remains tied to the state of ihram, requiring charitable expiation for injuries such as blinding or breaking horns, thereby linking ritual purity with tangible social responsibility.
